She is also a very strict leader who enjoys keeping order. She likely not only knew who the message was for (which the scene seems to confirm), but also for the sake of avoiding excessive awkwardness amongst the swim team opted to immediately break the tension by barking orders so people were going back to their regular business and not frozen by the oddity of the MC's profession.

While Morishima is arguably a pervent on the level of the main character (which is what makes their interactions so great), Ai instead plays as someone who encourages the main character's perverted tendencies. Her early interests and notice of him come as a result of either situations that are misunderstood to be perverted (needing to use the rest room), or which are actually quite perverse (the swim club fiasco).

The second half of your comment is more correct than the first, but I'll get back to that later. I'll assume you know what corporatocracy means, because it's pretty simple. So it must be the libertarianism part that lacking or misunderstood. And honestly, a few key points of libertarianism mostly understood, but looked at in a vacuum... I understand how corporatocracy could make sense as a perceived natural conclusion. But it's not.

There are a few, even more important, points that must be understood to know why it's impossible.

  • In a pure Libertarian society, the government has to answer to people, not corporations. The "weakest" person has more power than the "strongest" corporation in that regard.
  • As a follow up to that, only people have rights. Yes a corporation is a collective of people, but their rights do not act in aggregate, and can not ever supersede the rights of an individual. Just like no individual's rights can never supersede another individual's rights.
  • The government would be so severely limited compared to what we have now, that it would be of no benefit to a corporation to try and control it. Specifically, at a federal level, that would basically be just national defense, foreign relations, and disputes between states. It's the billion other things they dip their fingers into that make them a desirable target to be corrupted.
  • When something bad happens through the "actions" of a corporation, those actions were done by people, decisions were made by people, and it's people that are held accountable. People acting on behalf of a corporation cannot act with impunity because of the anonymity of a corporation.

I'm cutting it short here because I can tend to blather on. But if there's something specific you'd like to talk about/explore further, I'm more than happy to.

One final thought though. If you replace the word corporatocracy with anarchy in your comment, it would be a more appropriate comparison to communism/authoritarianism. But please keep in mind that anarchy doesn't mean what most people think it means. Most people think it means "no rules", but it actually means "no rulers"; and the difference isn't merely semantics.
